uncited: Primitive Geometry is the foundational family of splatting methods that decompose volumetric data into explicit geometric or parametric primitives (such as voxels, tetrahedra, or line segments) which are transformed and rasterized in screen space [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].
It differs from ray-casting by computing contributions per primitive rather than per pixel, leveraging hardware-accelerated rasterization for real-time performance [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Primitive Representation:** The volume is decomposed into primitives.
These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware [S1, S3, S4, unofficial].

Each primitive $k$ is defined by its position $\mathbf{p}_k$, density/extinction coefficient $g_k$ or $\rho_k$, and a reconstruction kernel $h$ (typically a Gaussian) [S1, unofficial][S6][S10, unofficial].
**Transformation:** Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp) [S2, S3, S4, unofficial].
For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening [S6][S10, unofficial].
**Rasterization:** The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane.
This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending [S1, S2, S3, S4, unofficial].
**Compositing:** Contributions are accumulated to form the final image.
This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly [S1, S2, S3, unofficial][S7, book].
Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time) [S10, unofficial].
**Hardware Acceleration:** Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity [S1, S2, S3, unofficial].
